title: Maersk Just Launched a New Shipping Route From Shanghai to Gujarat. India's Trade Deficit With China Is the Reason.
excerpt: The FI2 service deploys six container ships carrying 4,500 TEU each. Pipavav port's rail link to Delhi makes this more than a shipping route — it is a supply chain shortcut for India's biggest trade partner.
body:
Maersk, the world's largest container shipping company, has launched a new direct service connecting three Chinese ports to western India. The first vessel on the FI2 route departed Shanghai on June 4, marking a significant expansion of shipping capacity on the China-India trade corridor.

The service deploys six container ships, each carrying approximately 4,500 TEU — the equivalent of roughly 2,250 standard 40-foot containers per vessel. Ships will call at Shanghai, Ningbo, and Nansha in China before sailing to Malaysia's Tanjung Pelepas transshipment hub, Mumbai's Nhava Sheva port, Gujarat's Pipavav port, and Port Qasim in Pakistan.

## Why Pipavav Matters More Than Mumbai

The route's most consequential feature is its stop at Pipavav, a port in Gujarat that most Indians outside the shipping industry have never heard of. Pipavav is India's first public-private partnership port terminal and, critically, the first port connected to the country's Dedicated Freight Corridor rail network.

That rail connection means cargo arriving from China can move directly from the ship to a train and reach the National Capital Region — Delhi, Gurugram and Noida — in roughly two days, bypassing the congested roads and fragmented logistics that typically add days and cost to moving goods from India's western ports to its northern industrial centres.

For e-commerce platforms like Amazon and Flipkart, which depend on fast restocking of Chinese-manufactured goods, the Pipavav connection could meaningfully reduce fulfilment times. For manufacturers sourcing components from China, it offers a more predictable supply chain.

## The Numbers Behind the Route

The new FI2 service exists because the trade it serves is enormous and growing. In the financial year ending March 2026, India's imports from China rose 16% year-on-year to approximately ₹12.64 lakh crore ($150 billion). India's exports to China grew faster — up 36.66% to about ₹1.87 lakh crore — but from a much smaller base.

The result: India's trade deficit with China widened to a record ₹10.81 lakh crore ($128 billion), up from ₹9.52 lakh crore the previous year. China remained India's largest trading partner, a distinction that sits uncomfortably alongside India's stated goal of reducing dependence on Chinese manufacturing.

The imports are concentrated in sectors that India cannot easily substitute domestically. Electronics components, telecom equipment, active pharmaceutical ingredients, industrial machinery and solar cells account for the bulk of the trade. These are inputs to Indian manufacturing, not finished consumer goods — which means restricting them would directly raise costs for Indian producers.

## Hormuz Factor

The new route also carries an implicit insurance value. With the Strait of Hormuz blockade disrupting shipping patterns across the Indian Ocean, alternative and additional capacity on east-west trade routes has become strategically valuable. While the FI2 route does not pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the broader disruption to global shipping has increased demand for dedicated services on routes that remain open.

Maersk's decision to add capacity on this specific corridor — rather than redeploying vessels elsewhere — signals the company's bet that China-India trade volumes will continue to grow regardless of the geopolitical environment.

## What It Means for India's Manufacturing Ambition

The irony of a new shipping route designed to make Chinese imports cheaper and faster reaching India is not lost on policymakers. India's Make in India programme and Production-Linked Incentive schemes are explicitly designed to reduce import dependence, particularly on China.

But the reality is that India's manufacturing sector still depends heavily on Chinese inputs. The smartphones assembled in Noida use Chinese screens and chips. The solar panels installed in Rajasthan use Chinese cells. The pharmaceutical tablets exported from Hyderabad start with Chinese active ingredients.

The FI2 route operates alongside Maersk's existing FI3 service, giving shippers more frequency and flexibility. For India's economy, it is a reminder that the country's manufacturing ambition and its trade dependence on China are not contradictions that can be resolved quickly — and that the infrastructure to manage that dependence is, for now, more valuable than the aspiration to end it.
nri_angle: For NRI entrepreneurs and import-export businesses with India operations, the new route reduces transit times for Chinese components that power everything from electronics assembly to EV manufacturing. E-commerce platforms like Amazon and Flipkart will benefit from faster restocking, which matters for diaspora-funded D2C brands selling through these marketplaces.
